references.title: Geogram: a programming library of geometric algorithms

filters.name: Mesh Union (geogram)
filters.shortDescription: Create the exact union of two mesh layers using geogram.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown: Computes the exact boolean union of two mesh layers and creates the result as a new layer, using geogram's exact predicates. Both operands should be closed, consistently oriented surfaces without self-intersections; *Repair Self-Intersections (geogram)* can prepare an input that is not.

parameters.label: First Mesh
parameters.help: First operand of the boolean operation.

parameters.label: Second Mesh
parameters.help: Second operand of the boolean operation.

parameters.label: Simplify coplanar facets
parameters.help: Merge facets that end up coplanar in the result. Turning this off keeps every triangle the intersection produced, which is larger but preserves the original tessellation more closely.

filters.name: Mesh Symmetric Difference (geogram)
filters.shortDescription: Create the exact symmetric difference of two mesh layers using geogram.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Computes the exact boolean symmetric difference (XOR) of two mesh layers and creates the result as a new layer.

geogram's boolean evaluator provides union, intersection and the two differences, but not the symmetric difference, so this filter composes it as $(A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)$. That is **three** boolean evaluations rather than one, so expect it to take roughly three times as long as *Mesh Difference (geogram)* on the same operands. Both operands should be closed, consistently oriented surfaces without self-intersections; *Repair Self-Intersections (geogram)* can prepare an input that is not.

parameters.label: First Mesh
parameters.help: First operand of the boolean operation.

parameters.label: Second Mesh
parameters.help: Second operand of the boolean operation.

parameters.label: Simplify coplanar facets
parameters.help: Merge facets that end up coplanar in the result. Turning this off keeps every triangle the intersection produced, which is larger but preserves the original tessellation more closely.

filters.name: Repair Self-Intersections (geogram)
filters.shortDescription: Remove self-intersecting faces and retriangulate the holes using geogram.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Attempts to make a surface conformal by removing intersecting faces and retriangulating the holes they leave, using geogram's exact predicates. The result is created as a new layer.

The pass is repeated until no intersection remains or the iteration limit is reached, so a mesh with deeply nested intersections may need more than the default number of iterations. This is the usual way to prepare an input for the geogram boolean filters, which require operands without self-intersections.

parameters.label: Maximum Iterations
parameters.help: How many times to repeat the remove-and-retriangulate pass before giving up.

filters.name: Parametrize by Least Squares Conformal Maps (geogram)
filters.shortDescription: Compute a Least Squares Conformal Maps UV parametrization using geogram.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Computes a Least Squares Conformal Maps parametrization of the current mesh and stores the result as per-vertex texture coordinates. LSCM minimizes conformal (angle) distortion with two fixed points, so the mesh must have a boundary. If the mesh already carries per-wedge texture coordinates they are synchronized from the new per-vertex ones, so the result is immediately visible in the texture and UV views.

This is the reference implementation, by the authors of the original paper.

The flattening follows the mesh's existing vertex connectivity: coincident but distinct vertices stay split and appear as a seam, so run *Remove Duplicate Vertices* first on a mesh loaded from a format that does not share them, such as STL.

filters.name: Parametrize by Angle-Based Flattening (geogram)
filters.shortDescription: Compute an ABF++ angle-based UV parametrization using geogram.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Computes an ABF++ (Angle-Based Flattening) parametrization of the current mesh and stores the result as per-vertex texture coordinates. ABF++ solves for the flattened *angles* rather than the vertex positions, which generally yields noticeably lower angle distortion than LSCM on the same input, at a higher cost. The mesh must have a boundary. If the mesh already carries per-wedge texture coordinates they are synchronized from the new per-vertex ones.

This is the reference implementation, by the authors of the original paper.

The flattening follows the mesh's existing vertex connectivity: coincident but distinct vertices stay split and appear as a seam, so run *Remove Duplicate Vertices* first on a mesh loaded from a format that does not share them, such as STL.
